about.intro: My name is Nuria Guevara Fuentes and I'm a Full-Stack web developer. I currently work as a web developer and I'm studying a Master's Degree in Web Development with AI at The Big School and Universidad Isabel I. This page exists to answer, in detail and in first person, the question a one-page CV usually leaves unanswered: who I am, what I've built, and what I can bring to a team or a project.

sections.title: Who I am
body: I'm a Full-Stack web developer. I work on both frontend and backend, I enjoy understanding a project end to end — from architecture to interface — and I don't settle for the first solution that works: I look for the one that holds up in the medium term. Before web development, I spent over a decade working in communication; it's an anecdotal chapter in my day-to-day work now, but it left me with a habit I still apply when coding: understanding who and what I'm building something for before anything else.

I'm curious by nature. I enjoy solving a logic problem in JavaScript just as much as digging into a new technology until I really understand it, and I'd rather be the person who understands a project end to end, from the architecture down to the last detail of the interface.

sections.title: My path into web development
body: My formal entry into web development was the Full-Stack bootcamp at IMMUNE Technology Institute (2023–2024), where I learned to build complete web applications with React, Node.js and MongoDB, design interfaces with Chakra UI, animate with Framer Motion, and set up REST architectures with Express and JWT authentication. It was an intense learn-by-building process: a new technology every week, and a real project to put it to the test. The bootcamp's final project was SafeMap, a collaborative risk-zone map for travelers, which is still one of the projects I've learned the most from.

After the bootcamp, I decided to formalize and deepen that knowledge with the Higher Degree in Web Application Development (DAW) at Universidad Alfonso X El Sabio (2024–2026), where I did an internship and built my Final Degree Project, Past In Pixels, which my supervisor described as unique, creative and groundbreaking. Right now I'm continuing my training with a Master's Degree in Web Development with AI, in collaboration between The Big School and Universidad Isabel I, because in this field training never really ends: technology keeps changing, and standing still isn't an option.

sections.title: My professional experience
body: I currently work as a web developer at the company I joined after finishing my internship for the DAW degree. There I develop and maintain web projects in a real professional environment, working with different languages and frameworks depending on each project's needs, including WordPress and AI-applied development. I also mentor new interns — a role my own company has described as an already indispensable part of the team's workflow.

In parallel, I've worked as a freelancer for Advokatkontoret.es (2025), where I redesigned key sections of the website, implemented multilingual support without relying on plugins, and created and edited audiovisual content for the platform.

Before web development, I spent over a decade working in communication — as a community manager, a reporter and a press officer. It's an anecdotal chapter in my day-to-day work now, but it left me with a habit I still apply: always understanding who and what I'm building something for before writing the first line of code.

sections.title: Technologies I work with
body: Day to day I work with JavaScript, HTML and CSS as a foundation, React on the frontend, and Node.js with Express on the backend, usually with MongoDB or MySQL as the data layer depending on what the project needs. I've built JWT authentication, designed interfaces with Chakra UI and Bootstrap, and added animations with Framer Motion when the user experience calls for it. I also work with PHP — my first project in this language was Eagles in Spain — and with WordPress, which I use daily in my current role.

I round out that stack with Python, Postman for testing and documenting APIs, and Git and GitHub for version control, plus Laravel. On occasion I also use digital analytics tools like Google Analytics or SEMrush, an extra that comes from my previous stage in communication.

sections.title: The kind of projects I enjoy
body: I especially enjoy projects that aren't just a technical exercise but solve a real problem and have their own identity. SafeMap was born from a very specific question — do we actually know how to move safely around a place we don't know? — and became a full collaborative application, built with React, Node.js, MongoDB, Express and JWT, where users flag dangerous or low-accessibility areas to help other travelers.

Past In Pixels, my Final Degree Project, is the project I'm proudest of: a web experience built with React that fuses history and technology, described by my supervisor as unique, creative and groundbreaking. I also particularly enjoyed building Eagles in Spain, my first PHP project and an intermodular project for the DAW degree, dedicated to the Spanish community of Philadelphia Eagles fans — proof that a technical project can simply be born out of a hobby.

In general, I'm drawn to projects where I can be involved end to end: understanding the goal, proposing the architecture, building the interface and solving the technical problems that come up along the way. That's why I still enjoy experimenting with different formats, like PalMotion (a fitness app built with Python and Streamlit) or Movie Selector (a small JavaScript app that consumes an external API to recommend movies).

sections.title: How I approach problems
body: Faced with a problem, my first instinct is to investigate rather than assume. When something doesn't work, I don't assume I already know the cause: I read the error, reproduce the bug, check the documentation and rule out hypotheses one by one until I find the real root cause, not just the symptom. It's a verification discipline I bring from my previous stage in communication — checking before assuming — but that I apply exclusively to code today.

It also helps that I'm not afraid to say I don't know something yet. In a field that keeps changing, pretending to know everything is the fastest way to stop learning. I'd rather acknowledge the current limit of my knowledge and get to work on closing it — which is exactly the idea behind the phrase that best sums up how I work.

sections.title: My philosophy
body: "There's no such thing as 'I don't know', only 'let's find out how'." This isn't a slogan — it's literally how I've built my career. I went from not knowing how to code to building complete Full-Stack applications because, every time I hit a limit, my response was to find a way past it — a bootcamp, a higher degree, a master's, a new freelance project — instead of accepting the limit as final.

I apply that same philosophy inside every project: if I don't yet know a specific technology a project needs, that's not a blocker, it's just the next item on the list. And I firmly believe in something that still holds true in development: a project's value isn't only in the numbers or the lines of code, but in the experience it creates for the person using it.

sections.title: How I work
body: I work methodically: I like to understand the full context of a project before writing the first line of code — who's going to use it, what problem it solves, what technical constraints I'm working within — and document the important decisions as I go.

I'm comfortable working independently — as in my freelance projects, where I manage the project end to end — and within a team, where I currently also mentor colleagues who are joining. I pay particular attention to technical communication within the team: explaining decisions clearly, documenting what I build, and keeping everyone in the loop on progress.

sections.title: What I bring to a team
body: I bring real technical ability in Full-Stack development: I can build a feature end to end, from architecture to interface, and document it so the rest of the team can follow along. I also mentor interns at my current company, which pushes me to explain technical decisions clearly, not just make them.

On top of that, as an anecdotal differentiator, I bring over ten years of prior experience in communication: I understand why a feature matters to the end user, not just how to build it. And above all, I bring the attitude summed up in my work philosophy: faced with any new challenge, my default response is to find out how to solve it, not to explain why it can't be done.

sections.title: What I'm looking for professionally
body: I'm looking for projects and teams where I can keep growing as a Full-Stack developer: React, Node.js and the technologies I work with daily, in environments where well-built code matters as much as the result it produces. I'm especially interested in everything related to web development applied to artificial intelligence, the area I'm currently expanding my training in through the Master's at The Big School and Universidad Isabel I.

If you have a project, an opening, or just want to talk about web development, you'll find my details on the contact page. And if you ask me whether I know how to do something I haven't fully mastered yet, you already know my answer: there's no such thing as 'I don't know', only 'let's find out how'.

pastinpixels.title: Past In Pixels
pastinpixels.description: Final degree project, described by my tutor as unique, creative and ground-breaking. An interactive map to explore history through art, built with React, Node.js and seven external APIs.
pastinpixels.seoDescription: Case study of Past In Pixels, Nuria Guevara's final degree project: an interactive art and history map with React, a Node.js backend and museum, Wikipedia and Wikidata APIs.
pastinpixels.problem: The final project of the Higher Technical Degree in Web Application Development had to prove I could build, on my own, a complete web application with its own identity. I chose a real problem: history and art are usually learned separately and without geographic context, when an artwork makes far more sense once you know where and at what historical moment it was created.
pastinpixels.goals: Build a Full-Stack application that placed artworks and historical events on an interactive map, let users search them by bringing together data from several museums and open sources, and allowed each user to create their own narrative tours.
pastinpixels.architecture: React frontend, built with Vite and deployed on Vercel, with React Router and protected routes for signed-in users and administrators. A custom Node.js backend, deployed on Render, exposes a REST API for users, token authentication, tours and their artworks, and admin statistics. The frontend combines that API with seven external services: the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Europeana and Art Institute of Chicago collections, the Wikipedia REST API in Spanish and English, SPARQL queries to Wikidata and Google Maps.
pastinpixels.technologies: React, Vite, React Router, Node.js, REST API, Google Maps API, Wikidata (SPARQL), Wikipedia API, Met Museum API, Europeana API, Art Institute of Chicago API, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
pastinpixels.challenges: The biggest challenge was unifying very different data sources: each museum returns information in its own format, some APIs require a key and any of them can be slow or fail. On top of that, artworks and events had to be geolocated to be drawn on the map, and a user system with roles had to be designed without losing sight of the creative, visual side the project called for.
pastinpixels.solution: Searches run in parallel across the three museums with Promise.allSettled, so if one source fails the others still return results, and duplicates are then removed to show a single list. Wikidata provides, via SPARQL, artworks and historical events with coordinates and dates, and Wikipedia adds a summary for each one in a context panel. The Node.js backend handles sign-up and login, profiles, tours (with their artworks and personal notes) and a super-admin panel to manage users, with private and admin routes on the frontend as well.
pastinpixels.result: A complete, published Full-Stack application where anyone can explore history through art on a map and save their own tours. My tutor described it as unique, creative and ground-breaking, the highest qualitative recognition any of my academic projects has received.

safemap.title: SafeMap
safemap.description: Collaborative map where users flag dangerous or low-accessibility areas to help travelers.
safemap.seoDescription: Case study of SafeMap, Nuria Guevara's Full-Stack bootcamp final project: a collaborative map built with React, Node.js, MongoDB, Express and JWT.

safemap.label: bootcamp final project
safemap.p1: Traveling and exploring the world has become commonplace today. Distances feel short and the interconnected world we live in lets us visit places that, not long ago, could only be dreamed of.
safemap.p2: But once we're there — do we know how to get around? How do we get back without running into accessibility issues or dangerous areas?
safemap.p3b: : a map where users can place "red flags" on public spaces or streets to warn other users of the application.
safemap.seoDescription: SafeMap: a collaborative risk-zone map, Nuria Guevara's Full-Stack bootcamp final project, built with React, Node.js, MongoDB, Express and JWT.
safemap.problem: Traveling to unfamiliar places is increasingly common, but it isn't always easy to know which streets or areas have safety risks or accessibility issues before arriving.
safemap.goals: Build a collaborative application where any user can flag risky or low-accessibility areas on a map, to help other travelers move around with more information.
safemap.architecture: Full-Stack application: React frontend with Chakra UI and Framer Motion animations, Node.js backend with Express following a REST architecture, MongoDB database, and JWT authentication.
safemap.technologiesList: React, Node.js, MongoDB, Express, JWT, Chakra UI, Framer Motion.
safemap.challenges: Designing a collaborative geographic data model and secure JWT authentication within the tight timeline of a bootcamp final project.
safemap.solution: Full development of the application as part of the IMMUNE Technology Institute bootcamp team, covering frontend, backend, database and authentication end to end.
safemap.result: Final project of the IMMUNE Technology Institute Full-Stack bootcamp (2023-2024), deployed and functional.

react.name: React
react.seoDescription: Three years with React, my favourite framework: the foundation of my final degree project (Past In Pixels) and my bootcamp capstone (SafeMap).
react.intro: React is my favourite framework and the one I almost always choose when I get to decide a project's technology. I've been working with it for three years, first during my training and now in my day-to-day professional work.
experience: I started with React intensively at the IMMUNE Technology Institute Full-Stack bootcamp (2023-2024) and haven't stopped using it since. The projects that closed both stages of my training are built with React: SafeMap, my bootcamp capstone, and Past In Pixels, my final project for the Higher Technical Degree in Web Application Development.

In SafeMap, React drives a collaborative interface where users log in, browse a map and flag risky or low-accessibility areas, talking to a custom REST API built with Node.js and Express. Past In Pixels was a different challenge: building a visual, narrative experience that blends history and technology, where a component architecture let me keep content, presentation and animation separate.

I still work with React today and, whenever I can choose the stack, it's the first option I propose. This very website is an example: it's built with React, React Router, Chakra UI, i18next for bilingual support and a prerendering step so search engines can read every page.
practices: Reusable components with clear single responsibilities
State management with hooks, plus custom hooks for reusable logic
Routing with React Router and lazy-loaded pages with React.lazy
Internationalisation with i18next, with copy kept out of the code
SEO for React apps: per-page metadata and prerendering
Accessible interfaces combined with Framer Motion animations

sections.title: Why React is my first choice
paragraphs: What I value most about React is that it makes you think of the interface as small, predictable pieces. A well-scoped component is easy to understand, test and reuse, and that pays off when a project grows or when someone else has to pick up the code.

Its ecosystem matters a lot too: React Router for navigation, component libraries like Chakra UI, Framer Motion for animation or react-helmet-async for SEO. Almost every need already has a mature solution, which leaves time for what makes the product unique.

sections.title: How I structure a React project
paragraphs: I split the code into pages, reusable components and a utilities folder for logic that doesn't depend on the UI: configuration, structured data and custom hooks. Copy lives outside components, in translation files, so adding a language or fixing a sentence doesn't mean touching JSX. And pages that aren't needed on the first visit are lazy-loaded with React.lazy and Suspense.

nodejs.name: Node.js
nodejs.seoDescription: Node.js underpins Nuria Guevara's projects: REST APIs in SafeMap and Past In Pixels, JWT authentication, and scripts and build tooling.
nodejs.intro: Node.js sits underneath all my projects: as the server when there's a backend, and as the development and build environment when the frontend takes centre stage.
experience: My most complete Node.js project is SafeMap, my capstone for the IMMUNE Technology Institute Full-Stack bootcamp. There I built the entire backend with Node.js and Express: the REST API consumed by the React frontend, user sign-up and login with JWT, and the MongoDB connection that stores users and risk zones.

In Past In Pixels, my final degree project, I used Node.js for the backend again: a REST API deployed on Render that manages users, token authentication, custom tours with their artworks and notes, and an admin panel with statistics and user management.

But Node.js is there even when there's no custom server. My whole frontend workflow depends on it: dependency management with npm, dev servers, builds and custom scripts. On this website, for instance, I use Node.js scripts to generate the sitemap automatically and to prerender every page before publishing it.
practices: REST architecture with Express
Authentication and authorisation with JWT
Separate routes, controllers, models and middlewares
Configuration and credentials in environment variables
Endpoint testing and documentation with Postman
Node.js scripts to automate build and deployment tasks

sections.title: How I structure a Node.js backend
paragraphs: I split code by responsibility: routes that define endpoints, controllers with each request's logic, models that describe the data, and middlewares for cross-cutting concerns like authentication or error handling. Credentials and configuration live in environment variables, never in the code.
Before wiring up the frontend I test every endpoint in Postman, so when something breaks I know whether the problem is in the API or the interface.

sections.title: Why Node.js
paragraphs: Using JavaScript on both server and client removes much of the friction of Full-Stack work. And the npm ecosystem means tasks like authentication, validation or database access have proven solutions, so I can focus on the product logic.

javascript.name: JavaScript
javascript.seoDescription: JavaScript underpins all of Nuria Guevara's projects: frontend with React, backend with Node.js and vanilla JavaScript apps like Movie Selector.
javascript.intro: JavaScript is the foundation of everything I build. If React is the skeleton of my applications, JavaScript is the muscle: logic, data and interaction all run through it.
experience: I work with JavaScript every day, on the frontend alongside React and on the backend with Node.js. Using the same language on both layers lets me move across the whole application without switching context, apply the same validation rules and reason about data end to end.

Before relying on frameworks I wanted to master the language itself. Movie Selector is a good example: a vanilla JavaScript app with no libraries that queries an external movie API, handles the asynchronous responses and renders the result to the DOM. Projects like that teach you what a framework actually does for you.
It's also there in projects where another language takes centre stage: in Eagles in Spain, my first PHP project, JavaScript handled the frontend interactivity.
practices: Vanilla JavaScript when a project doesn't need a framework
Asynchrony with async/await and explicit error handling
Consuming external APIs with fetch
Modular code with ES Modules and small functions
Immutable work with arrays and objects (map, filter, reduce, spread)
Version control with Git and GitHub

sections.title: What mastering JavaScript means to me
paragraphs: It isn't just knowing the syntax but understanding how the language behaves: asynchrony with promises and async/await, variable scope and closures, immutability when working with arrays and objects, and the differences between the browser and Node.js.
That knowledge is what lets you debug an error the framework doesn't explain, decide when a library is unnecessary or write code someone else can read effortlessly.

sections.title: Modern JavaScript, every day
paragraphs: I write modern JavaScript (ES6+): modules, destructuring, arrow functions, array methods like map, filter and reduce, and fetch to talk to APIs. I keep code modular, with small functions and clear names, and version it with Git and GitHub.

php.name: PHP
php.seoDescription: Nuria Guevara's experience with PHP and Laravel: from Eagles in Spain, her first PHP project, to professional use alongside MySQL.
php.intro: PHP is one of the backend languages I work with, both plain PHP and Laravel, and always paired with MySQL.
experience: My first contact with PHP was Eagles in Spain, the cross-module project of my Higher Technical Degree in Web Application Development: a website for the Spanish community of Philadelphia Eagles fans. I learned the language from scratch while bringing the requirements of several subjects together in a single project.

Since then I've kept working with PHP professionally, in an environment where different languages and frameworks coexist depending on the project. There I've worked both with PHP more generally (maintenance, new features, frontend integration) and with Laravel when a project calls for a fuller structure.
PHP is also the language WordPress runs on, which I work with every day too, so understanding what sits underneath the CMS helps me go beyond plugins.
practices: MVC with Laravel: routes, controllers, models and Blade views
Prepared statements and input validation
Migrations to version the database schema
Separation between business logic and presentation
Integrating a PHP backend with HTML, CSS and JavaScript

sections.title: Plain PHP and Laravel
paragraphs: Plain PHP gives me full control over every request and is a good fit for simple sites. Laravel brings what a bigger project needs: routing, the MVC pattern, the Eloquent ORM for database work, migrations to version the schema and Blade templates for views.
Having started with PHP without a framework helps me understand what Laravel solves under the hood, which makes debugging and decision-making easier.

sections.title: PHP and MySQL
paragraphs: In my PHP projects the database is MySQL. I use prepared statements to prevent SQL injection and, in Laravel, migrations and Eloquent to keep schema and data consistent.

wordpress.name: WordPress
wordpress.seoDescription: Nuria Guevara's experience with WordPress in her current role and in freelance projects.
wordpress.intro: WordPress is part of my daily work in my current role.
wordpress.experience: In my current role I develop and maintain web projects with WordPress as part of my regular work. I've also used it as a freelancer to redesign key sections of the Advokatkontoret.es website, where I also implemented multilingual support without relying on plugins.
practices: Redesigning sections without breaking the rest of the site
Multilingual support without relying on extra plugins
Maintenance and development in a professional environment

mysql.name: MySQL
mysql.seoDescription: MySQL is the database behind Nuria Guevara's projects: relational schemas and SQL in apps built with PHP and Laravel or with React and Node.js.
mysql.intro: MySQL is the database I use in my projects. When data has clear relationships (users, content, categories, orders), a well-designed relational database is the most solid choice.
experience: I learned relational database design during my Higher Technical Degree in Web Application Development, and since then MySQL has been the database I work with day to day, both in PHP and Laravel projects and in JavaScript applications with React on the frontend and Node.js on the backend.

My work with MySQL ranges from designing the data model to everyday queries: defining tables, primary and foreign keys, relationships between entities, and writing queries that return exactly what the application needs.
practices: Normalised relational schema design
Foreign keys to guarantee data integrity
SQL queries with JOINs, aggregations and subqueries
Indexes on frequently searched columns
Prepared statements to prevent SQL injection
Laravel migrations to version the schema
MySQL access from Node.js APIs for React applications

sections.title: How I design a database
paragraphs: Before creating a single table I think about the entities and how they relate. I normalise the schema to avoid duplicated data, use foreign keys so the database itself guarantees integrity, and choose each column's type carefully. A good initial design saves a lot of trouble as the application grows.

sections.title: MySQL in JavaScript and React applications
paragraphs: In React applications the frontend never talks to the database directly: it goes through a Node.js and Express API, which connects to MySQL, runs the queries and returns the data as JSON. That keeps credentials and data-access logic safely on the server, while the React interface only requests and displays information.
Working with the same relational model from PHP or from JavaScript lets me pick the backend language that best fits each project without giving up a solid database.

sections.title: Queries and performance
paragraphs: I write SQL with JOINs to combine tables, GROUP BY aggregations and precise filters, and I add indexes on the most frequently searched columns. From both PHP and Node.js I always use prepared statements, and in Laravel I rely on Eloquent and migrations to version the schema alongside the code.

sections.title: MySQL vs MongoDB
paragraphs: I've also worked with MongoDB, but for most projects I prefer MySQL: relationships between data are explicit, transactions guarantee consistency and SQL is a standard language any developer can read.

mongodb.name: MongoDB
mongodb.seoDescription: Nuria Guevara's experience with MongoDB: SafeMap's database in the Full-Stack bootcamp and practice projects with Node.js and Mongoose.
mongodb.intro: MongoDB is the NoSQL database I've used to learn the document model and understand when it fits better than a relational database.
experience: I learned it during the IMMUNE Technology Institute Full-Stack bootcamp, where it was part of the stack alongside Express, React and Node.js, and I used it in SafeMap to store users and the risk zones flagged by the community. Since then I've kept building practice projects to go deeper into how it works.
My main database is MySQL, but working with MongoDB has given me another way of thinking about data and lets me choose the right tool for each project with good judgement.
practices: Document-oriented data modelling
Schemas and validation with Mongoose
Choosing between embedded documents and references
Integration with Express in a REST API

sections.title: What working with documents taught me
paragraphs: MongoDB stores data as flexible, JSON-like documents, which fits naturally with a JavaScript application. With Mongoose I defined schemas and validation to keep some structure, and learned to decide when to embed information inside a document and when to reference another one.
In SafeMap, each flagged zone is a document with its location, description and the user who created it, a structure MongoDB handles very naturally.

sections.title: When I'd choose MongoDB
paragraphs: I'd pick it for loosely structured or frequently changing data, quick prototypes, or applications where each record is fairly independent. For highly relational data that needs strict consistency, I still prefer MySQL.

api.name: API / REST
api.seoDescription: Nuria Guevara has built and consumed REST APIs since she started coding: JWT backends in SafeMap and Past In Pixels, plus museum, Wikipedia and Wikidata APIs.
api.intro: I've worked with APIs since I started programming. Building and consuming them is a core part of my Full-Stack work: it's what connects an interface to the data that gives it meaning.
experience: My two most complete training projects revolve around APIs. In SafeMap, my capstone for the IMMUNE Technology Institute Full-Stack bootcamp, I built a REST API with Node.js, Express and JWT authentication that manages users and the risk zones flagged by the community.

In Past In Pixels, my final degree project, I went a step further and combined both sides. On one hand, the app has its own Node.js backend with a REST API: user sign-up and login, profile, custom tours with their artworks and an admin panel with statistics, all protected with Bearer tokens. On the other, the React frontend consumes several public cultural APIs at once: the Metropolitan Museum of Art collection, Europeana and the Art Institute of Chicago to search for artworks, Wikipedia and Wikidata to enrich them with historical context, and Google Maps to place them on a map.
I've also consumed APIs in vanilla JavaScript projects such as Movie Selector, which queries an external movie API to recommend a film, and they remain part of my everyday work.
practices: REST endpoints organised by resource
Authentication with JWT and Bearer tokens, plus role-based admin routes
Consuming several APIs in parallel with Promise.allSettled and graceful failure
Unifying and de-duplicating data from different sources
SPARQL queries to Wikidata for structured data
Centralised client-side calls with single-point error handling
Endpoint testing and documentation with Postman

sections.title: Combining several APIs into one experience
paragraphs: The most interesting challenge in Past In Pixels was unifying sources that look nothing alike. Each museum returns data in a different shape, some APIs need a key and others don't, and any of them can be slow or fail. I fire the searches in parallel with Promise.allSettled, so if one source fails the others still show results, and then remove duplicates so the user sees a single, coherent list.
For each artwork's context I use the Wikipedia REST API in Spanish and English and SPARQL queries to Wikidata, which return structured data such as artists, dates and places.

sections.title: How I design my own API
paragraphs: I organise endpoints by resource (users, tours, artworks) with clear, predictable routes, and use HTTP methods and status codes for what they actually mean. Private routes require a token in the Authorization header, and admin routes are reserved for users with that role.
I test and document every endpoint in Postman before wiring it to the frontend, and on the client I centralise calls in functions that add headers and handle errors in one place.
